rationale: I'm switching the features from the referential montage to the clinical neonatal double-banana bipolar montage (18 derivations), with a 0.5–30 Hz zero-phase band-pass applied before features are computed. Bipolar derivations remove the shared reference signal, which mixes artifacts and remote activity into every channel. They also bring out focal, rhythmic seizure activity in one region. The filter removes drift and high-frequency muscle noise, which otherwise dominate line length and RMS.

I'm adding per-neonate normalization. Each channel's log features (line length, RMS, band powers) are robust-z-scored against that recording's own median and interquartile range (IQR) before taking max/median across channels. These normalized aggregates are kept alongside the raw ones. Background amplitude and spectra vary a lot between neonates, and seizures are focal, so a channel that rises well above its own baseline should separate seizures from background better than absolute levels do. This uses no labels: each recording is normalized only with its own data.

Amplitude and band-power features can't tell a rhythmic seizure discharge from a high-amplitude artifact or busy background. I'm adding three rhythmicity / spectral-shape features to each channel: normalized spectral entropy, the fraction of power in the dominant 0.5–8 Hz peak, and the largest autocorrelation after the first zero crossing within lags of 2 s. The autocorrelation is computed from the 0.5–30 Hz band-limited, zero-padded spectrum. Each feature is then summarized as max, median and min across channels, which matches the regular, narrow-band, focal look of neonatal seizures.

Neonatal seizures last tens of seconds and change gradually, but each per-second feature currently sees only its own 8 s window. This change adds centered moving averages of all 27 features over 15 s and 61 s windows, so the classifier sees evolving trends over time and transient artifacts are averaged out. The moving averages are label-free and computed within each recording.

The background EEG drifts within each recording, with sleep-state changes, medication and electrode changes. A seizure shows up as an evolving departure from the neonate's recent background, not as an absolute level. Round 2's global per-recording z-scoring was discarded, so this time I add relative features that are local in time. For each of the 27 channel-aggregated features, I compute its 15 s moving average minus its centered 10-minute rolling median. The raw and context features stay unchanged.

I'm replacing the single global classifier with a per-channel detector, the approach used by the published neonatal SVM systems. Each row is now one channel-second: that channel's 27 features (its 9 features plus 15 s and 61 s context averages), its difference from the cross-channel median, and the cross-channel median and max, so the model can still see the background. The seizure probability for each second is the maximum over the 19 channels, then smoothed over 10 s. Taking the max, median and min of each feature separately, as now, mixes values from different channels, so a focal discharge's coherent signature on one channel is lost. Scoring each channel as a whole and then taking the max fits seizures that are focal, rhythmic and confined to one region. For speed, training uses every 4th second.

Consecutive seconds are highly autocorrelated (8 s windows plus 15/61 s context), so the training set holds only about 63 independent neonates, not ~300k independent rows. With 20-sample leaves and lr 0.1, the default HGB can memorise neonate-specific background patterns. I'm regularising it towards rules that hold across neonates: leaves of at least 2000 seconds, 15 leaves per tree, lr 0.05 over 500 iterations, L2 = 1 and per-feature binning unchanged. The goal is better neonate-independent ranking in the concatenated AUROC.

Neonatal EEG has a steep 1/f background, so the raw-spectrum peak fraction and the autocorrelation are biased toward slow delta activity. A seizure, by contrast, is a narrow-band rhythm that stands out above that background. This change fits a line to log power vs. log frequency over 0.5–30 Hz in 0.5 Hz bins for each channel and second. It adds three features per channel: the largest residual peak in 0.5–8 Hz, that peak's frequency, and the background slope. Each is aggregated as max, median and min across channels and gets the same 15 s and 61 s context averages as the existing features.

This adds spatial-synchrony features to tell spatially spread artifacts from focal seizures. Each second gets a 19×19 inter-channel correlation matrix from the 0.5–30 Hz band-limited spectrum. From it come the global synchrony (largest-eigenvalue fraction), the mean absolute correlation, and each channel's mean absolute correlation to the others (max/median/min). Artifacts that reach every channel, such as ECG and movement through the common reference, look rhythmic and high-amplitude to the current per-channel features but are highly synchronous across the montage. Neonatal seizures are focal and synchronous only locally, so these features should separate the two. The new features also get the existing 15 s and 61 s context averages.

I'm replacing the fixed 10 s moving-average post-processing with a learned second stage, while keeping the 10 s smoothing on top. Inner grouped 3-fold CV gives out-of-fold first-stage seizure probabilities. A small, heavily regularized gradient-boosting model then learns from multi-scale trajectories of those probabilities (5–301 s centered means and 15/61 s running maxima of the logit). Neonatal seizures are sustained, evolving events, while artifacts give isolated or erratic spikes in probability, so a learned temporal model should rank seconds better than a fixed smoother.

I'm changing only how training seconds are weighted: within each class, a second's weight becomes proportional to 1/sqrt(the number of seconds of that class in its neonate). Each class keeps its original total weight. Right now a few neonates with long seizure runs (some have hundreds to thousands of seizure seconds) dominate the positive class, so the model learns their particular discharge morphology. Neonates with short focal seizures barely count, which hurts ranking across neonates. Rounds 7 and 8 suggest the model is sensitive to neonate-specific idiosyncrasies, so evening out each neonate's influence should help more than adding features.

All current features are confined to 0.5–30 Hz, so artifacts that look rhythmic or high-amplitude in that band can't be identified. This mainly means muscle/EMG, which is broadband and strong above 30 Hz, and movement or sweat drift, which sits below 0.5 Hz. Both are major false-positive sources in non-seizure neonates and hurt the concatenated AUROC. I'm adding two artifact-indicator log band powers to each channel: 0.125–0.5 Hz and 30–45 Hz (staying below the 50 Hz mains frequency). Like the other per-channel features, each is summarized as max, median and min across channels and gets the 15 s and 61 s context averages.

The training set holds only about 63 independent neonates, so one HGB fitted to all of them learns some patterns specific to individual neonates' backgrounds, and that variance hurts ranking on unseen neonates. The new solution trains 8 HGBs, each on a random 75% of the training neonates (bagging by neonate, with a fixed seed for each model), and averages their probabilities to reduce that variance. Features and the 10 s smoothing are unchanged.

All channel features currently come from the referential montage. The common reference spreads activity from one region into every channel, which blurs the focal, local seizure discharges that clinicians read on the neonatal double-banana. This change keeps everything that exists now and adds the same 9 per-channel features, computed on the 18 double-banana bipolar derivations and aggregated as max/median/min, with the same 15 s and 61 s context averages. The derivations are built linearly from the existing FFT, so there is no extra filtering, which round 1's discarded version did apply, and very little extra compute.

Context features gave the biggest gain so far (round 4), which suggests seizure evidence builds up over tens of seconds. The fixed 10 s post-smoothing was never tuned and may be far too short for Helsinki's long seizures, so this change picks the smoothing width from {1, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80} s by grouped 3-fold inner CV on the training neonates, scored by concatenated AUROC. To save time the inner fits use every 2nd second, and smoothing now repeats the edge value instead of padding with zeros, so probabilities no longer dip at the ends of a recording.

At the moment the 15 s and 61 s context averages are taken after collapsing across channels, so a 15 s average of the max mixes evidence from whichever channel was highest each second. A sustained focal discharge on one channel gets diluted by that mixing. This change also averages each channel's 9 features over time first, and only then takes the max, median and min across channels. That gives "the most persistently rhythmic or high-power channel" features, which match focal, evolving neonatal seizures. These 54 new features are added alongside the existing ones, which stay unchanged.

I'm adding the third-largest channel value of each of the 9 per-channel features as a new cross-channel aggregate, alongside max, median and min, and it gets the same 15 s and 61 s context averages. Neonatal seizures are focal but usually show up on a few neighbouring electrodes. A max over channels is easily set off by one bad electrode (electrode pops, single-lead artifacts), so a top-3 statistic should be a more robust focal-seizure signal that most single-channel artifacts don't reach.

I'm adding the two Hjorth descriptors used in the classic neonatal seizure detectors (Temko/Tapani) to every channel: mobility and complexity. Both come from spectral moments of the 0.5–30 Hz band-limited signal (m0, m2, m4 of the spectrum already computed). Mobility tracks the dominant frequency, and complexity is close to 1 for a pure sinusoid, so together they give a cheap measure of how waveform-like the signal is. That should help separate rhythmic seizure discharges from irregular background and artifacts. Like the existing features, they are aggregated as max/median/min/3rd-largest across channels and get the 15 s and 61 s context averages.

I'm replacing the single histogram gradient boosting model with an equal-weight average of it and a strongly regularized ExtraTrees model, keeping the same features. ExtraTrees uses random splits and leaves of at least 30 seconds, so it should vary less between neonates. Small changes have moved the score by 0.01–0.03, which points to the HGB model latching onto features of individual neonates' backgrounds. Averaging in a more stable, different kind of model should give a steadier ranking across neonates in the concatenated AUROC. The smoothing width is still chosen by grouped inner CV, now on the ensemble's output.

I'm adding a third centered moving average of every per-second feature over 181 s, alongside the existing 15 s and 61 s ones. Round 4's context features gave the biggest gain so far and the tuned post-smoothing tends to favour wide windows. Helsinki seizures often last minutes, so a near-3-minute summary should help tell sustained, evolving rhythmic discharges from short artifact bursts. Like the existing context features, it is label-free and computed within each recording.
